FRIDAY EVENING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JULY 18
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Prime Minister is going to make a statement in introducing his motion?

subtopic: FRIDAY EVENING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JULY 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement I intend to make will be quite short. I know from long personal experience that the lengthening of the sittings to a six-day week makes it a trying experience for all members of the house, and I did realize that situation when I introduced this motion. Each year, however, it becomes necessary, as we begin to arrive at a point when we can look forward with some hope to the end of the session, to introduce a motion similar to this.
I think I should say a word or two with regard to the industry and the application of members generally in the discharge of their responsibilities as members of this house. Like the weather, the shortcomings of politicians provide a never-ending subject for discussion, and we receive selective treatment from time to time in that many feel there is not that degree of application which there should be with respect to the responsibilities of our official positions. With that viewpoint I entirely disagree. I know there are exceptions to every rule, but I know of no other group of public servants or people generally who more diligently and honestly devote themselves to the discharge of the work that is theirs in the interests of the public welfare. In saying this I believe, however difficult and trying it is for those who devote themselves with earnest application to the problems which come before the house and in committees, that the time has now come to make this motion.
57071-3-138
The legislative program as forecast in the speech from the throne has not been entirely carried out. In addition to those matters which are already on the order paper there are a number of matters which are in process of being made ready for placement on the order paper. There are therefore quite a number of matters which still require to be considered. I would be the last to in any way endeavour to unduly activate members into getting on with the business, but I feel that the committees to which assignments of estimates have been made should make a special effort to report on their examination of such estimates at the earliest possible date, so those estimates may receive the further consideration of the committee of the whole house.
It has been suggested by a number that it might be a good idea to adjourn until the fall. I feel that generally speaking hon. members would like to see the business concluded before adjournment. That is the objective and the purpose of the government and, I trust, of members in general. The matters that are still to come up are of singular importance, but I feel that with the extension of the hours of sitting of the house to the degree set out in the motion, a first step will have been taken to ensure the completion of the agenda with the greatest dispatch without-and I emphasize this-in any way doing anything that will savour of pressure being applied to bring about an early end to the session.
I do believe that if this motion is passed- and I commend it to all members in all parts of the house-it will be the first step along the road to the termination of the session after the completion of the business in hand.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FRIDAY EVENING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JULY 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of the official opposition do not intend to oppose this motion, which in its terms does not go quite as far as some of us had been led to believe it might.
We are as anxious-perhaps not as anxious as the members of the government with the additional responsibilities they have to bear- but we are as anxious as other hon. members of the house to conclude the business of the session with the least possible delay. It is true, of course, that with the number of committees now sitting, together with the work that has to be done in the house itself, a very considerable burden is imposed on all members of the house and particularly on members of the opposition groups, but I should

Business of the House
like to reassure the leader of the house that we are not complaining about that.
One way in which the business of the house could be facilitated and, I think, expedited, would be to have it more effectively organized in advance so that we might know in advance what we are going to deal with. I recall, and I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite recall, the words of the former leader of the Conservative party when he sat on this side of the house as leader of the opposition, when he was accustomed to reproach the government in season and out of season, two or three times a week, because, he said, we had not organized our work properly. I commend his words to hon. gentlemen opposite at this time. If they would give us a little more advance notice of what is coming up perhaps we would be able to play an even more effective part than we do now toward expediting and facilitating the work of the House of Commons.

subtopic: FRIDAY EVENING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JULY 18
speechtext:
We in this group intend to oppose the motion, because we feel that we have not yet begun to arrive at a point when, as the Prime Minister said, we can look toward the end of the session.
I think the job of members of parliament is to come here and to arrange the business of the house and perform their duties in such a way as to give each item the consideration that it warrants. I feel that this being the first full session of parliament since 1956, the time has not arrived when we should endeavour to speed up the session as is contemplated by this motion.
I have examined the motions that have been presented in sessions gone by which provided for an extension of the hours of sitting of this house, and I believe I am correct when I say that since the end of the war-and that is as far back as I have gone- such a motion has never been brought in during any full session of the house at as early a date as that at which the present motion is being put forward.
In 1946 almost five months of the session had gone by before a motion was brought in to extend the hours of sitting. In 1947 over five months had elapsed before such action was taken. In 1948 over seven months had gone by before such a motion was brought in. The present session is barely two months old, yet a motion to extend the hours of sitting has already been presented. In 1951 the session was almost five months old before a similar motion was presented. In 1952 four months had elapsed, in 1954 seven months had elapsed, in 1955 six months had elapsed, and in 1956 approximately six and a half months had elapsed before the motion extending the hours of sitting was brought down.

As a matter of fact I think we are a long way from the point where we can really say we see the end of the session as far as business being dealt with by the house is concerned. Almost all the estimates have still to be brought before the house. Only the estimates of the Department of Public Works have been dealt with at any length, and I do not believe that consideration of even that department's estimates is yet completed. As far as the work outlined in the speech from the throne is concerned we have barely scratched the surface. Among other things the throne speech referred to a bill of rights. I do not know if the government intends to go forward with its bill of rights, but that certainly has not been brought before us.
The throne speech forecast further amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act to be introduced at a later stage of the session. Such items as the construction of a railway to Great Slave lake, the provision of roads for development in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, the South Saskatchewan river project and the proposal respecting the establishment of a new agency to regulate broadcasting in Canada and to ensure that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and privately owned broadcasting stations work effectively together have not been introduced. The new National Capital Act, the act to provide for cash advances, amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, the Canadian Farm Loan Act, the Ticket of Leave Act and a number of other pieces of legislation forecast in the speech from the throne and to which I have not referred in detail have not been brought before us.
There are a great many committees of the house now sitting. Today a meeting has been called of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping to sit at 9.30 a.m., 3.30 p.m. and 8.00 p.m. A meeting of the committee on mines, forests and waters has been called for 10.30 a.m. The estimates committee is meeting at 11.00 a.m. At the very time when hon. members of this house are exceedingly busy with a great many committees that are meeting we have brought before us a motion of this kind, and still the estimates must be dealt with during this session.
I am quite prepared to work as many hours as I am able to during a given week, and I believe that is true as far as all hon. members are concerned; but I also feel that we should be given a chance to work as efficiently, and effectively as possible. It would seem to me as far as the deliberations, of the house and meetings of committees are concerned that five full days, starting in the morning and going through to evening sessions on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, makes a very full week.

As far as week ends are concerned, as far as Friday evening and Saturday are concerned, most hon. members spend that part of their time in preparing and briefing themselves for the work of the week ahead.
I do not think hon. members can give the estimates proper scrutiny, I do not think they can deal with legislation as carefully as it should be dealt with, if they are to be put under the kind of pressure that comes from sitting six days and four evenings a week, along with morning sittings of a great many committees of this house.
I do not understand the government putting this kind of pressure on members of the House of Commons so early in the session. Because not since 1956 have we had a full session of parliament, I think this kind of motion should have been delayed until the session had been going on for four or five months, as was the case when other similar motions have been presented during similar sessions in the past.
For many years members of parliament were paid a sessional indemnity. At that time it was assumed that a session would be short. For a short period of time members would leave their normal occupations, come to Ottawa and deal with, public business. But after sessions had become much longer the whole basis of pay of members of parliament was changed. We all agreed that it was an improvement. Today members of parliament are paid each and every month of the year. I believe that step was taken to pay members on a yearly basis because it was recognized that being a member of the House of Commons is really no longer a part time job; it is a full time job, and it is the kind of job that takes between five and six and close to seven months of the year in Ottawa during a session properly to discharge the work that is put before the House of Commons.
We are opposed to this motion, Mr. Speaker, as I said, not because we expect it will mean any more work for our group- I do not see how it could-but because we feel that members of parliament generally are now working to maximum capacity, and it is the kind of pressure that makes it impossible for members to do the work of the house as they should. If after another week or two the government should bring in another motion to extend further the sittings of this house it would make a mockery of parliament itself, because how is it possible for members to do the work on committees and carry on the sittings of the house on an extended basis and still be able to say in good conscience that the work has been dispatched carefully and with consideration?

Business of the House
The government, along with the Leader of the Opposition, should be doing a better job of planning the work of the session itself. When this motion is dealt with and after the orders of the day are called we shall be considering a fifth supply motion. The rules in the rule book provide for six supply motions during the session. When a few years ago the number of supply motions was limited to six, it was then understood that those supply motions would be brought in periodically so that periodically throughout the session members would have the right to raise grievances before supply was granted. There will only be one further supply motion left after the one set for today has been dealt with. The whole purpose of supply motions has been abrogated and sidestepped. The rights of members to raise grievances before going into supply will be removed. That is one way in which planning has not been adequate or even within the spirit of the rules.
The rules also provide for six private members' Mondays. If we are in sight of the end of the session, as the Prime Minister says, I wonder whether it is the intention or hope that the session will end some time before all private members' Mondays have been called and that by cramming the session into a short period of time private members' days will not be proceeded with. I for one believe that these rules were placed in the rule book only after careful consideration, and I believe they should be complied with in spirit as well as in letter.
It would seem to me that the government is showing undue haste by presenting this motion for extended sittings now, by speeding up the calling of supply motions and by leaving the whole question of private members' days very much up in the air. Because we believe in a more careful and diligent study of public business, Mr. Speaker, we in this group intend to oppose the motion.

session is likely to last, but in view of this motion this is the beginning of the end, I think the house is entitled and will want to know what is in the mind of the government with reference to future legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FRIDAY EVENING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JULY 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is arranging to get the details to reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Laurier. I intend to take but a few moments on the motion to deal with some of the points raised by the hon. member for Assin-iboia. The weakness of his argument is apparent when he says that this is the type of session which should last for six or seven months. That would mean until November or December. I suggest that any such plan would be not only unwise but also unreasonable.
Let us turn our minds back to what has happened within the last 18 months. A session was held in the spring of 1957 when the former government was still in office, and a portion of the business for 1957 was completed at that time. I believe the whole 10 days were allowed for the debate on the speech from the throne. Other time was allowed for supply motions and a certain amount of time for private members' days. I do not remember the exact number of days, but all the preliminary work involved in a regular six-month session was done at that time.
Then there was the election in June and the new parliament met in October. At that time again there was a 10-day debate on the speech from the throne. We had a certain number of supply motions. We had a number of private members' days. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, this provision for six two-day supply motions and for six Mondays plus two Thursdays for private members was designed for an ordinary session of the duration of six or seven months. But we have not been in that position at all, and we are not in that position today.

This impossibility of arriving at an agreement on any short-cuts is the responsibility of members of the C.C.F. Today we would have been debating external affairs had the government and the official opposition been able to carry out what they wished to do, but the eight members of the C.C.F. in the corner would not agree. They would not

agree to waive one of the private members' Mondays in order that we could discuss external affairs.

Here we have the proposal made today that this session should go on for six or seven months. I believe the vast majority of members of this House of Commons believe that their duties as members are not confined to being in Ottawa for 12 months of the year. They have an equal responsibility to be out in their constituencies meeting the people they represent and finding out what are the problems which face their people.
This procedure would be absolutely impossible if the plan put forward today by the leader of the C.C.F. were followed. This house would continue in session. There would be no adjournment for the summertime. He did not provide for any adjournment; oh, no, he said six or seven months. That takes us right into December. Then the government has the duty of calling a 1959 session probably in January, and certainly not later than early February, in order that next year's business may be done. Incidentally I may say that we hope to be able then to get the business of parliament back on the regular basis whereby work would be finished within a period of six or seven months, all the provisions for full supply motions and private members' days could be carried out and the business of the house completed in the ordinary manner.
Mr. Speaker, I have never yet known it to be possible to conclude the business of this

house without sitting extra hours. That certainly was the case when we were in opposition. We did not like having to sit extra hours any more than the hon. member for Assiniboia likes it, but how many hours has the house been sitting thus far? It has been sitting 25J hours a week. This rule was changed because the majority of the members of the House of Commons lived within a short distance of Ottawa and they wanted to go home for the week ends. Let us have no misunderstanding about that matter. I do not blame them. I would probably be the same if I lived near Ottawa. The rule was changed so that we sat from 11 o'clock to one o'clock on Friday morning, thereby taking away one day for committee sittings, and we did not sit on Friday evening. As a result members from the far west and those from the far east had to sit around here all week end, unable to do any business, because the majority of the members wished to go home.
The result, of course, was that the sessions lasted that much longer and the arrangement was unfair to those who lived a long way from Ottawa.
The government today is only asking members to sit to consider estimates on Friday nights and Saturdays; nobody is going to be hurt. If a lot of members want to go away for the week end, let them go; but I do not believe very many will do so. I believe that the sense of responsibility among the members of this house is so great that a comparatively small number would not be here to do the business of the house on Friday nights and on Saturdays in the same way they would be here on any other week day. We are not infringing on the rights of parliament. We have great respect for the rights of parliament. We have experienced in the flesh what it means to have those rights interfered with.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister in his introductory remarks was kind enough to say some good words about members of parliament as a group. When I heard this buttering-up, Mr. Speaker, I knew the blow was going to fall later on but I would like to do a little buttering-up myself in relation to the performance of Conservative members.
This is a new House of Commons and we have a tremendous number of new members who are receiving their initiation. There are a great many committees now meeting. One of the epithets which the Prime Minister hurled at the Liberals a few years ago was they were a collection of trained seals; in fact, I believe this term acquired the dignity of no longer being considered unparliamentary. I think with respect to the untrained seals we have at the present time, we have pretty good evidence that the performance of Conservative backbenchers both in the house and with respect to their fairly active part in committees is an improvement upon the performance of the Liberal backbenchers when the Liberals were in office.
This indicates that there has been a real interest on the part of Conservative backbenchers during this session, and I would suggest that those members are going to suffer just as much as are the members of the smaller opposition groups by the introduction of these extended hours.
I would like to raise another point, which I think is important, and that is that in my opinion the members from the far west and far east of Canada have been carrying the burden and will be doing so even more under these new hours of sitting. The Minister of Public Works can say that the members from these areas do not like to lie around here on the week ends doing nothing, but from my own observations of these members they have been the ones who to a great extent have carried the load in this House of Commons, especially on Fridays and Mondays. They look forward to a break at the week end as much as anyone else in order to do their office work, and it is always remarkable to me to find so many western and eastern members around the house on Saturdays and Sundays catching up on their work and their studying. I would say that the present motion would make their difficulties even greater.
I am particularly interested in the official opposition's attitude toward this motion. This seems to stem from the fact that in recent months there has been a good deal of castigation with respect to the Liberals by the press. They have been criticized for their poor attendance during the last session and previous sessions. This is the only explanation of which

I can think for the stand announced by the Leader of the Opposition.
I would like to point out that the factors which make us object to this measure-which make us obstructionists, if you will-should be just as important to the official opposition, because it is much easier for the members on the government benches to carry on the work in committees than it is for opposition members. It has been particularly difficult for members of this group to cover all the committee work. I think the Liberals' conduct with respect to this particular motion, in consenting to go along with it rather than vote against it, can only be explained by the fact that their consciences must be bothering them and they are afraid of a renewal of comments in the press on their performance in parliament during the recent past and the amount of work carried out by them.
We have just had two election campaigns and recently a high pressure session. These provide further reasons for taking a fairly slow pace at the present time, in my opinion, because I can think of nothing more exhausting for members of parliament than election campaigns. Why increase the pressure now by means of extra hours at the end of the week?
In closing my remarks I would like to refer to some remarks of Hon. George Drew when he was a member of the opposition in this house with respect to this particular point. The Minister of Finance discovered last year, when he mentioned to the house the tremendous number of hours he was working, that he got scant sympathy from the house and from the country. We get very little sympathy by telling people how hard we work. I do not want to express either personally or on behalf of this group or on behalf of members of the house any similar complaint, but these are the words of Mr. Drew which I would like to leave with hon. members for their consideration. On January 2, 1955, as quoted at page 4344 of Hansard, Mr. Drew said on a motion to extend the hours of the house the following:
I do not think it is in the interests of parliament to convey to the public the idea that we are prepared to accept hours which will deny appropriate attention to public business merely in an effort to get out of here by the end of June.
If I might interject, it seems that this is what the Minister of Public Works implies; that we could not possibly stay here until the end of November or December but that we must get out of here as quickly as possible.
If the public business demands that we stay longer, let us stay longer.
And this is the point I wanted to emphasize:
Let us make sure, however, that we follow a course that is within both the physical and mental capacity of hon. members, having regard to the

immense amount of work still before us. Let us also be sure that we do not disregard the impression that would be conveyed by a very sparse attendance while billions of dollars of public funds are being voted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has built quite a reputation over the past couple of years as the champion of the rights of parliament. In fact I believe he has built up for himself the reputation of being the very symbol of the rights of parliament in this country. We therefore find it very difficult to reconcile that picture with the motion now before us. He has for long maintained that the most important thing in parliament is that the opposition should have the opportunity and privilege of functioning properly, in fact that parliament must always be ensured of such an opportunity.
While on this side of the house the Prime Minister on many occasions pointed out that the proper functioning of parliament depended just as much upon Her Majesty's loyal opposition as it did on the government itself, if not more. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, though he did hedge round the question as to just how many times the Conservative opposition passed up their rights, would find, if he took the trouble to look through Hansard, that it is not very often that members of the Conservative party when they sat on this side of the house left any stone unturned to ensure that their opposition was a vigorous one and was going to do a job. Actually the duty of the opposition is not only a privilege; it is a duty. The opposition is duty bound, by the form of government we have, to study, examine and criticize proposed legislation and to suggest any alternatives to government legislation which is introduced in the house.
We have at the present time the smallest opposition we have ever had and certainly this is a time, if ever there was a time, when the privileges of the opposition should be protected with great care. I have noticed several occasions during this very session when this house has been divided on a question and when there were more than enough government members missing on a vote to have outvoted the combined opposition if we were all present. And this is only in the short period during which we have been sitting so far. What will happen from now on if we are going to have to sit Friday nights and Saturdays is anyone's guess, but the fact remains that half or three-quarters of those on the government's side can take their week ends off, but not so the members of the opposition. If we are going to do the job which it is within our power to do and which we are in duty bound to do, we are going to have to attend in the future, as we have attended in the past.
Business of the House
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Assiniboia, this is the earliest time in any session on record, I believe, that such a motion has been introduced into the house.
I wonder if it is only pure coincidence that the earliest record of such a motion coincides with the greatest government majority that has ever been seen in the parliament of Canada. We feel there is no need of this motion at the present time. There may be need of it in the future, and if a time comes when it is needed, that will be another matter. But we feel that at the present time it constitutes an imposition on the opposition which they are physically incapable of meeting. I note that at the present time we have to try to go 30 hours a day in order to try to get 24 hours in, and with this in mind, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskam-ing (Mr. Peters), I should like to move the following motion:
That the resolution be amended by eliminating the words "and Saturday", and by eliminating all the words after "10.00 p.m." up to and including the words "Thursday (government day); and", and also by eliminating the words "2(1) and".

amended now, it is allowed by the rules. But in each case where there was a debate on the address there was a different government in power. I repeat the statement I made earlier that this is a regular session of parliament, that we have before us the whole of the estimates, and that, as the first session in a new parliament, it should be the attitude of the government to co-operate in every way possible to allow full discussion and to allow the full time provided under the rules for both private members' Mondays and for motions on going into supply, and with regard to all the other rights of the House of Commons.

of move for the extension of sittings should be brought in. We say that the rule book is clear on the subject. Mr. Speaker, I am rising to say that we do not feel we can support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin). The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) expressed certain surprise that the official opposition did not take the same line he was taking in his speech. I suggest that perhaps the reason the official opposition did not take the same line as the hon. member for Port Arthur is that the official opposition has had the experience and the responsibility of carrying on the government of this country and expects to have it again, and that one's attitude to the deliberations of this house and to the work of parliament is unquestionably affected by considerations of that kind.
If the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had carried out the intention that we understood the government originally had to take away the time in the mornings on ordinary sitting days and thereby interfere with the deliberations of committees-and I think with my leader that there are too many committees trying to sit at once at the present time for the efficient operation of parliament -we would have joined with our friends to my right and to your left, Mr. Speaker, in resisting this motion but I do not think they have made out a case for refusing to sit on Saturdays.
I agree with the leader of the house-and this is about the only respect in which I do agree with what he said-that we should spend some time in our constituencies if we hope to represent our constituents properly in this parliament. I feel that if by sitting on Saturdays we can dispose of some of the estimates of some of the departments we are justified in doing this. But I do not feel it is any reflection on parliament if every one of the 265 members is not present when the estimates of each of the departments-for instance, the Department of Fisheries-are being considered. I simply give that as an illustration and I consider that as important a department of government as there is.
If we are going to do our duty in this parliament that does not mean all of us have to be in our places in committee of supply when the estimates of every department are

under consideration. There has to be some division of labour, and I use the term in the classical sense. It seems to me perfectly proper for the house to sit on Saturdays, at this stage of the session, in order to consider estimates. I would hope that the government would not attempt to do anything else but take up estimates on Saturdays, because to attempt to proceed with legislation on Saturdays would be an abuse of what the government is asking us to do. For the purpose of taking up the estimates it does not seem to me that a case has been made against the proposal of the government.
I must say there was one other thing with which I agree in what the leader of the house said and that was his indirect and implicit commendation of the way in which Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris conducted the business of this house when they had charge of the leadership of the house. If the hon. member will look at the comments he made regarding the first session of 1957 he will see that he paid them a high compliment, but I am afraid I cannot reciprocate. It seems to me that the leader of the house is still, in spirit, on this side of the house. He is far too provocative. He does everything possible to obstruct the business of the government. As a very young member to a very old member I would suggest to him that he try to get through his head that he has won two elections and that he now sits on the government side of the house and is the leader of the house and therefore he should attempt to be conciliatory if he wants to get the arrangements of the house made in a fashion to expedite business-

Business of the House
I think it is only reasonable and logical, as was pointed out by a member of the official opposition a few moments ago, to say that there is a great deal of work to be done outside of the House of Commons, if we are to accept our responsibility, but we have not the time to do it. There is a limit to what members can do; but even beyond that there is something that should never be forgotten by an elected member and that is this. We are making laws, changing laws or rescinding laws. Because we deal with questions that mean so much in the way of taxation and the expenditure of money-and do not forget it is going to be around $6 billion this year-we should be in a position where we can do that work not only expeditiously but efficiently and with cool, calm deliberation and with a full knowledge of exactly what it is we are doing.
It is for that primary purpose that I oppose the motion which we are now discussing and which was introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). Through you, Mr. Speaker, because you were also here, I want to remind him of the hours, the days and the weeks, and I think I can say the months, that a select standing committee of this house spent on the revision of the standing orders. The committee was finally able to come to conclusions and bring in recommendations at a session of a previous parliament. The changes made in the standing orders were of such a nature as to expedite government business and to guarantee the time and rights of private members. I was here, Mr. Speaker, when that report was brought in and I heard all the debate. I recall how often it was pointed out that although some of the previous rights of private members were to be given over to government business for the expedition of government business, that in the 
standing orders there was the protection of the rights of private members.
My hon. friend, the Minister of Public Works, was one of the strongest advocates of, and always insisted on, the rights of private members and the fact that they were spelled out in the standing orders. Yet, now that he and others have crossed the floor they have forgotten a great deal about the protection of the rights of private members through the medium of the standing orders and exactly why the standing orders read the way they do. It was pointed out by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) that no matter how small a group may be the rights and privileges of private members are the rights and privileges of all members except those of the cabinet. If we look over the order paper, as was pointed out, I repeat, by the hon. member for Assiniboia, we see that the majority of the items that appear under private members' names appear under the names of private members from the government side of the house.

We in this group go over every resolution and every bill to study it and to reach a decision and we believe that we-it may seem strange-are rising in our places this afternoon and fighting on behalf of the rights of private members on the government side so that they may have an opportunity to discuss the things that they thought important enough from their point of view and their constituencies' points of view to place on the order paper of the House of Commons.

I have 96,000 people in my riding. We have every kind of organization meeting, on an average of one a day, and I contribute to most of them. I contribute as a member should, to fulfil my duty. I am very pleased to do it, but it takes half of my indemnity for that purpose. Hon. members who are far away have only to answer a few letters, and
Business of the House
tell their constituents that they cannot be in their ridings. This is about all that it costs you, and many of you ask for free airplane transportation. Many of you are lucky that you cannot go home to your riding. Do not try to fool us. I do not go home every night, my good friend. I have lived in Ottawa since I became a member. I go home once in a while, sometimes every two weeks. I have never lost more than two or three days during a session, and I have received and seen over 1,500 of my electors yearly.
I do not care how long we sit. When I first came here, we were sitting up until 11 o'clock or until 12 o'clock. I do not care how long we sit as long as the business is well done. I understand that we are a small group in the opposition-something which is too bad. The people misunderstood us the last time. I hope that they will understand us better the next time. I will sit here from any hour of the morning until any hour at night, and I am glad to do so in order to do our job properly. But let us not have committees sitting when the house is sitting in the morning because we cannot be here and attend the committees at the same time, as we are a small group in the opposition. I say to the C.C.F. that we do not need them to make an intelligent opposition. We have done it up to now and we are able to do it any time. We will do it in a constructive way in order to protect the Canadian people against too much bad administration by the government. Let us keep on working.

The obvious conclusion we reach, regardless of the smoke screen which was spread over this issue by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green)-and he is quite adept at doing this on any and every occasion-is that we have to rush into this legislative program not because we have a special situation arising out of two elections in a year, or arising out of an incomplete session prior to the election last year, or in minority government and so on, but because of the obvious frustration and restlessness that exists among the government's backbenchers. I know many of these private members personally, and have spoken with them, and they have indicated that they are frustrated-that they are restless-that they do not like being here because there is relatively little for them to do. So they want to get it over and go back to their law practices, or whatever it is, or rush back, as is right, to their constituencies to spend all the time possible at home, which we would all like to do. Obviously the Prime Minister is giving in now to this pressure from his backbenchers. I wish he had not done it so early in the session.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to oppose the motion proposed by the Prime Minister and I should like to state several reasons why. The leader of the house has accused us of being unfair to other members of this house. I feel that when the leader of the house placed on record the fact that this house was sitting presently for only 25J hours a week that he, unintentionally, was most unfair to all members of this house, because the minister, on reflection, will concede that the newspapers would love to headline the fact that some members of parliament object to working for more than what he calls a 25J hour-week. I ieel that if there was any unfairness this
Business of the House
afternoon it was this calling to public attention the records of Hansard and the fact that this house sits for 25J hours a week, when the minister himself is quite aware, from his many years of experience, that there is no such thing as a 40-hour week, a 50-hour week or even a 60-hour week for conscientious members of parliament who must work even longer hours than that.
Mr. Speaker, we in this group attempt to be fair to ourselves, to our responsibilities and to the problems that confront this parliament and the government of Canada.
I have in mind at this time especially the very serious problem to which practically no attention has yet been given during this session and that is the problem of heavy unemployment in the middle of the summer. I realize that not all hon. members find it necessary to spend an equal number of hours in their work as members of this house and it may well be that the hon. gentlemen in that party which has an overwhelming majority in the house may And it difficult indeed to work 60 hours a week. They may find that they like to-in the minister's words-go home for the week end.
I feel that the minister was further slightly unkind when he indicated that hon. members did not-to use his words again-like to sit around here. I presume he meant on week ends. I can assure him that there is not very much sitting around here on week ends; instead, there is a great deal of working around here on week ends and if the minister's memory is that short it might do him some good for him to be in the house on a week end and observe the many hon. members who are working.
This afternoon we have had a perfect example of the old policy between the government and the official opposition of "you scratch my back and I'll scratch yours". The desire to get out of the house and have done with the session seems to be shared by members of both the larger parties.
At this time I wish to enter a plea on behalf of a group other than ourselves. We all know what the regulations are and when the house sits on Saturdays the employees of the house must also work on that day. If this resolution receives the endorsation of the house-and I hope it will not-I trust some arrangement will be made whereby the employees will be assured of the continuation of the five-day week which they have enjoyed for the past several months. I feel that it is most unfair to expect these employees to work a six-day week merely to please our convenience so that we can have done with the session at as early a date as possible.

Business of the House The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) outlined a little of the history of the last several sessions of parliament. However, I should like to remind him that almost for the past two years this house has been largely engaged in political squabbles laying the groundwork for the election battles and not too much attention has been paid to the business of parliament. To illustrate what I mean one has only to think back and realize that this parliament did not complete the estimates for the year 1957-58. Indications are that we may have a difficult time indeed, if the wishes of many hon. members should prevail, finishing a consideration of the estimates of 1958-59. One of the most ancient rights and privileges of a people's parliament is for political purposes and now apparently for the sake of expediency to be shortened.
The public accounts committee has been constituted and as a member of it I have yet to receive notice of its first meeting. If the Liberals and Conservatives cannot agree as to who ought to be chairman I suggest that the government approach my leader with a view to inquiring if our group would consider appointing a chairman for the committee in order that we could get on with the business of the country. Some reality might be given to the much publicized role the public accounts committee would play under a Conservative regime. The select committee on broadcasting about which we heard so much in the speech from the throne has not yet been appointed to my knowledge.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) listed many pieces of legislation which were forecast in the speech from the throne but he omitted many of them which I intend to enumerate at this time. It was indicated in the throne speech that the government would attend the commonwealth trade and economic conference. Surely the parliament of Canada should be given an opportunity to express its views in this regard before that conference is held. The throne speech forecast an acceleration of useful public works projects designed to sustain employment but we have yet to hear of this accelerated public works program. It also forecast a public investment program but outside of the South Saskatchewan river dam nothing more has been heard. We in British Columbia were particularly awaiting some announcement of legislation by which means our province could participate in this program and I refer particularly to the Columbia river project but nothing more has been heard.
Forecasts were made of the extension of airports and air bases but we have heard nothing more of this. Mention was made in 
the budget as well as in the speech from the throne of amendments to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act but we have yet to see that legislation introduced. We were assured that amendments to the Financial Administration Act would be brought in but nothing has been done in this respect. We were assured by both the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that the House of Commons would be given an ample opportunity to discuss the government's use of warrants but no time has been allowed for such a discussion.
In conclusion I wish to offer the proposition that there is nothing so horrible in the thought of the House of Commons sitting, as the Minister of Public Works said, until November or even December. I believe that the people of Canada have the right to expect that we sit for as long as it is necessary to attend to the affairs of the greatest and hugest enterprise in Canada, the government and the business of the parliament of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: FRIDAY EVENING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS ON AND AFTER JULY 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to add to the festival that has taken place here this afternoon. Certain hon. gentlemen have reviewed the needs of parliament, the democratic system, the preservation of parliamentary rights and the necessity of having the legislative program passed by parliament. It is because we want to accomplish this that we have asked for the extension of the time within which this house will sit to the end that we may deal efficiently and effectively with the very large portion of the legislative program that still remains. There

are, however, some hon. gentlemen who believe that instead of having the division of labour which was referred to by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), their contribution to the solution of the problems that confront parliament is best determined by each of them saying the same thing over and over again. They choose to do this instead of having one or another of their members efficiently organized to the end that a full and proper discussion will take place.
Repetitious utterances, sir, do not solve problems or assist in their solution. I suggest to certain gentlemen who have spoken that possibly if they were better organized and those extra hours that they work had been devoted to allocating among members of their group responsibility to speak in respect of those subjects which they have studied more carefully than others, the business of parliament would be expedited and a considerable step taken toward making this house a place in which the determination of problems is on the basis of contributions rather than on measurement of the length of time taken by any of them on discussion and repetition.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) asked me to outline in general what will be brought before the house. I can do no better than refer to the speech from the throne. In it is contained the legislative program that we intend to bring before the house. It is because of the fact that so far the debates have been mainly on the speech from the throne and the budget, and not wishing to transgress the rights of private members to express themselves, the time has come, unless the House of Commons is to become the place in which the definition of eternity will be found, when we must act to the end that longer days, longer periods of sitting, will have to take place if we are to discharge our responsibility. That is why this preliminary motion is moved. It is not the complete picture, but at the moment committees are meeting. Because committees are meeting, and in an endeavour not to prevent those committees from completing their responsibilities, the extension is within the limited scope of this motion.
In so far as the legislative program is concerned, in addition to those things that appear in the speech from the throne, I might say that having regard to agricultural conditions on the prairies some further action is being considered by the government which, if determined in the affirmative, will require further legislation. So far as the Saskatchewan dam is concerned, the last word I have this afternoon is that the difficulties arising out of discussions by both sides have all but been resolved and my hope is that an agreement
Business of the House
will be signed by this government and the government of Saskatchewan which will, of course, necessitate legislation at this session of parliament to implement it.
Farther than that I do not intend to go. I do believe in the rights of parliament. Those rights shall be undiminished. That is the attitude of this government and that is the stand I outlined in the first speech I made in this house. But, sir, the legislative program must come before the house. If the normal hours at this period, in the passage of time since the speech from the throne, are insufficient, then there is only one way to proceed and that is the way we are following, the preliminary step, the minimum extension but not morning sittings, to the end that we shall be able to bring about a solution of our problems through the necessary legislative action.
Some speak about the rights of parliament. All I say is that these rights will be maintained. But at the rate the discussions are taking place here, where a few members believe that in order to show that they are making a contribution each says the same thing over and over again, the only way in which that can be met is to extend the time so that hon. members will have an opportunity to consider the matters that are of particular importance, as set out in the speech from the throne. Our objective is not to prevent members from talking; it is to extend the opportunity for that purpose. Instead of in any way interfering with members having the right to express themselves, I feel that the extension of time will enlarge those rights and I hope that ultimately in the process of time we will be able to have the legislative enactments on the order paper, not only placed before parliament but also passed by the house in its wisdom.
The program that we have is an important one. It has not been considered as yet with that degree of application on the part of all of us that I want to see, and I hope that when this motion is passed, if the house passes it, as I hope it will, we shall be able to make much progress because the work has been organized by the government. We are ready. Our legislative program is set out. The legislation is ready. We are now asking the House of Commons to proceed to consider that legislation and, I hope, to pass it.
My hon. friends talk about the house sitting until November or December. It is all very interesting. They speak disparagingly of others who have some responsibility. I hope the time never comes when we elect to the House of Commons only those who desire to spend 12 months a year here. I hope that we shall continue in the tradition of good parliamentary government and not prevent those who

Canada Conversion Loan can serve this country from serving because through unnecessary repetition we make it impossible to command and mobilize the candidature of those who can be induced to sit in the House of Commons, as many now sit, who, if they found that it was a 12-months job, would be unable to make their contribution to the building of a better Canada and the attainment of a better legislative program.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP CONVERSION LOAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an important announcement to make relating to our public debt operations. Today we are embarking upon the largest and I believe the most constructive financial operation in the history of Canada, of the successful outcome of which I am fully confident.
Hon. members are aware of the general background. In my budget speech four weeks ago I informed the house and the country in some detail of our financial requirements during the coming year. I stated then that in order to carry out our approved program in the fields of both economic capital development and social welfare we would require some $1,400 million of new money during this fiscal year, in addition to providing for the refunding of nearly $2,000 million of maturing bonds. This, as I said at that time, is a formidable task.
We must also look beyond the immediate needs of this fiscal year. During the next few years there will mature in quick succession the whole of the remaining wartime victory loans. The total amount of the five victory loans falling due between now and 1966 is over $6,400 million. This is a very large sum and it constitutes more than 60 per cent of our outstanding funded debt, excluding the special categories of Canada savings bonds and treasury bills.
This large volume of early maturities overhanging the market has made it very difficult
(Mr. Diefenbaker.l

to plan an orderly program of debt management and has contributed greatly to the general feeling of uncertainty which has prevailed in our bond markets for the past few years. This uncertainty in the market for prime Canadian bonds has had inevitable effects on the market for provincial, municipal and good corporate bonds.
We have therefore decided to clear away this heavy congestion of early maturities and to lay the foundations of an orderly and sensible program of public debt management. Today we are launching the Canada conversion loan of 1958. The details of this offer are being made public concurrently with this announcement. Holders of all unmatured victory bonds are being offered new and longer term bonds in exchange for their present holdings. The holders of the eighth and ninth victory loans maturing in 1963 and 1966 are offered a choice of new 4J per cent 25-year bonds maturing in 1983 or new 4|- per cent 14-year bonds maturing in 1972. Holders of the seventh victory loan which matures in 1962 may convert at their option into either of the two new bonds already mentioned or into a 3f per cent 7-year bond maturing in 1965. Finally, the holders of the fifth and sixth victory bonds due in 1959 and 1960 may convert into new 3 per cent 3|-year bonds maturing on December 1, 1961 or into any of the other new bonds mentioned.
In brief, the holders of all these victory loan bonds may convert into a choice of four issues, 25 years at 4J per cent, 14 years at 4i per cent, 7 years at 3f per cent or 3| years at 3 per cent, provided, however, that they must elect a bond which lengthens out to that extent their present term.
In addition, in order to adjust equitably the current market prices and yields of the old bonds to the new offerings we will make appropriate cash adjustments on conversion. Since we are making this offer to the two million individual private citizens who own these victory bonds, we are combining accrued interest and the cash adjustment into a single figure. The actual cash adjustment, exclusive of accrued interest, in favour of the person converting will depend upon the issue he is turning in and the new bond he is taking in return, but ranges from nil on the 1966 maturity being converted into the 14-year or 25-year bond to $1.99 per $100 par value on the 1959's which are converted into new bonds of 7-year maturity or longer.
This is not, of course, the first conversion loan in Canada's history. There have been a number of previous conversion loans relating to the victory loans of the first world war and of the second world war. But none of the earlier conversion loans has been on as

large or as comprehensive a scale as the one we are offering today. Detailed prospectuses will be in the hands of all branches of chartered banks and of all investment dealers either this afternoon or tomorrow morning.
This is a tremendous operation requiring the enthusiastic co-operation of everybody concerned. We spent long hours with officials and other experienced advisers under the leadership of the governor of the Bank of Canada perfecting our campaign plans and organizing committees. I am happy to report that I have received from all quarters pledges of enthusiastic and vigorous support in carrying this enterprise to a successful conclusion.
In the campaign I am now announcing the period between today and August 5 will be largely taken up with organization, but it will be open to any holder to deposit his old bonds and take his cash adjustment starting today. Our offer to convert will remain open up to and including September 15, 1958. All the new bonds will be dated September 1 and will bear interest from that date.
Apart from corporations and financial institutions it is estimated that there are two million private individual holders of the victory loan issues to which 1 have been referring. To make sure that each and every holder, in so far as it is humanly possible, is made aware of this opportunity we are arranging for a widespread publicity campaign using all appropriate media.
This conversion offer will perform the major and essential task of clearing the way for an orderly program of debt management over the years ahead. It will not, however, provide us with any new cash. To cover our cash requirements over the next few months we have arranged to sell an issue of $400 million of five-month bonds bearing interest at the rate of 2J per cent per annum to the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks. These very short-term bonds will fall due on December 15 next, a date which will coincide with our known cash receipts from this year's Canada savings bond campaign.
In conclusion may I say two things. The first is that we are convinced, and so are those with whom we have consulted, that this great conversion loan will lay the foundations for a new, healthy and confident tone to our whole bond market, and that the beneficial results of this will extend well beyond the market for Canada bonds and into the market for provincial, municipal and corporate bonds.
The second point I wish to emphasize is that this government attaches great importance and a high priority to the preservation
Canada Conversion Loan of a sound currency and stability in the purchasing power of our dollar. On behalf of the government I wish to reiterate that we intend to follow policies designed to maintain the soundness of the Canadian dollar.
Mr. Speaker, this is a great national undertaking. It is the concluding phase of the victory loan campaigns of the war years which, as we all remember well, enlisted the enthusiastic support of all Canadians. I confidently bespeak the support of all Canadians today in carrying through to a completely successful conclusion the Canada conversion loan of 1958.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP CONVERSION LOAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has indeed made a very important statement, a statement of an operation which was forecast in this morning's press and which, indeed, in its detail is in the afternoon press. As the minister has said, the Canada conversion loan, 1958, will be the largest operation of its kind in our history, even in our wartime history. He has emphasized quite rightly that for it to be successful it will require the enthusiastic co-operation of everybody concerned, and as I said in my contribution to the budget debate, Mr. Speaker, all Canadians will hope that he will get that co-operation and all Canadians must hope that this operation will be a success.
We in this country are entering upon some very difficult and complicated financing and refinancing moves which the minister has outlined to the house previously, and this is the first and a very important stage in what he himself has called a major financial operation. I repeat that we as Canadians must all hope that this operation will be a success and that, above all, the stability of our currency will be maintained throughout the operation. Of course, while all of us hope that, we cannot help but feel anxious about the effect on monetary policy and on inflationary pressures of the operation which is now beginning. We hope that effect will not be harmful, and we hope these inflationary pressures will be held in check. We will all be following with great interest the progress of this very important refinancing campaign.

Mr. Speaker, the announcement just made by the Minister of Finance is certainly one of the most important that has been made by a minister of finance since the end of the war. We hope with him that the objective of a sound money policy may be achieved and that the soundness of the Canadian dollar may be maintained. We hope also that the issues will be in smaller denominations so that ordinary

Canada Conversion Loan Canadians will have a chance to participate and that the terms of payment will be such that ordinary income earners will be able to acquire the bonds that are being issued. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MODIFICATION OF REGULATION OF NON-SCHEDULED SERVICES
speechtext:
In
view of the earlier comments of the Minister of Transport regarding competition between scheduled air line services, I wonder if he has also given any thought to possible modification of government regulation of non-scheduled services, particularly in the light aircraft field?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF REGULATION OF NON-SCHEDULED SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for advising me of his intention to ask this question. The answer to the hon. member's question is yes. The government, after study of this matter, has come to the conclusion that there should be an easing in the treatment of applications for licences for non-scheduled commercial air services which involve only the use of small light aircraft and helicopters.
The concept of regulated competition in the field of public utilities is already well

accepted as applying to public services which are of great importance to the population as a whole, or to major segments thereof. However, I can find no evidence to indicate that services provided by small, single-engine light aircraft and helicopters fall as a general rule within this category.
Services of this type can only offer transportation at a relatively high unit cost compared with larger aircraft. In total they provide only a small percentage of the air transportation picture in Canada. Nor is there any indication that the public interest would, as a whole, suffer if this type of air service was permitted to operate more freely. In fact all the indications are that the reverse would be the case, and the government has accordingly decided that it would be in the public interest that licences for air services using only this small type of aircraft be granted freely on request. This I consider to be properly in accord with the spirit of free enterprise.
I recognize that there may be a few instances, for example in remote northern areas, where the importance of services provided by this type of aircraft to a community is so great that, unlike in the settled areas of Canada, small aircraft service has to be classed as essential, and that in these cases the air transport board may vary the general policy I have indicated by bringing such cases to me for special consideration. I have informed the board, however, that I would expect instances of this sort to be very much the exception rather than the rule.
I have also informed the board that generally speaking this policy should apply to what is known as group C aircraft, that is small single-engine aircraft having a gross disposable load of less than 1,100 pounds and to small single-engine helicopters such as the Bell-47 and Sikorsky-51 types, but not to larger units.
