subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the fifth of the six supply motions we shall have this session, and I must confess that it is

Radio and Television
unfortunate that five of them will have been exhausted after today or tomorrow, because it looks as if we will now be here for some weeks, and I think it was the intention when standing orders were changed dealing with this matter that these supply motions would be spread as evenly as possible over the session.
I am not blaming anybody at the moment for this situation, but it does mean that after this supply motion has been exhausted we will have one only during the rest of the session. There may be very important developments during that time which would normally be raised by the opposition by moving amendments on going into supply, when such questions could be raised or grievances could be aired.
The subject I wish to raise today and on which in due course I will move an amendment is the question of national radio and television, which I think all members of the house will agree is an important aspect of national development, an aspect which leads us into the realm of the communication of ideas so important in welding together our sections and our people, in strengthening their unity and stimulating their pride in their country.
It is my view and the view of the official opposition that government policy should by now have been laid down with regard to this matter; that doubts and hesitations which have been created in recent weeks should be resolved, and that the house and indeed the country should know where we stand in this matter especially in view of the Fowler report on broadcasting and of the assurances given by the Prime Minister in the election campaign of 1957 and repeated in 1958 that the recommendations contained in that report would receive attention, as he put it, "at a very early date". Nothing has been done to remove this uncertainty, though I must add at once that we had a very interesting and very helpful statement by the minister concerned a few weeks ago.
Nothing, however, has been done to remove the uncertainty with regard to policy, an uncertainty which is bound to be felt in view of the strong position taken by the Prime Minister and by members of the government with regard to radio and television matters when they were in opposition. If we on this side of the house complain now of delay and uncertainty with regard to policy we should, I think, in all fairness, put forward our own views on this question and that is what I am proposing to do before I move the amendment.
In doing this I do not think I need stress at any great length the importance of radio and television in our national life, in the

development of Canadian culture, and in the development of a Canadian identity. They are two of our most powerful media for better or for worse in the pursuit of these essential goals. These days we hear a great deal about the special need at this stage of our history for a strong and healthy Canadianism. This is a matter of understandable concern to all Canadians. Therefore we are bound to be concerned with the performance of any agency for the communication of ideas such as radio or television, and with the contribution that such agencies are making toward the development of this strong and healthy Canadianism.
This is especially the case with broadcasting, because if we do not exploit this medium for right Canadian purposes and direct it in the public interest it will be used by others for purposes which may be good or which may be not so good, but which cannot be expected to be wholly Canadian. The national interest and a national purpose should be and have been, then, a responsibility for radio and television in this country, and this has been recognized by governments for many years. That interest is superior, and must remain superior, to any private advantage.
I suggest there must be no weakening of this principle in any policy that may be adopted in this house with regard to this matter. Control of our own air must help us to determine, in so far as any nation can so determine in this interdependent age, our national destiny, and help us develop our distinct national personality and our own Canadian culture.
Too much emphasis cannot, I think, be placed on the part that radio and television can play in building up on the northern half of this continent a distinct, cohesive, selfreliant national personality proud of its achievements and confident about its future without being smug or arrogant about it. Maintaining Canadian unity and building the Canadian nation has never been and perhaps never will be an easy task in the face of the geographic, economic and other factors that tend to separate us or pull us south rather than east and west. Canadian governments in the past of both parties have accepted the responsibility of countering these factors in the interests of national unity. They have accepted this duty in radio and television as they have in other forms of transportation and communications.
That has cost and will continue to cost us a great deal of money and I will have something to say about that a little later. We should not permit that cost to be one dollar higher than is absolutely necessary but I believe that what is determined to be

necessary by parliament should be given. That, in my view, would be a small price to pay for the results achieved in national or individual reward or satisfaction in the application of a good national television and radio policy.
Recently fears have been widely expressed and, I think, often deeply and genuinely felt that our own control over our economic life is being disturbingly and unduly weakened by our increasingly close integration with the economy of the United States, a process that has been going on in this country since the beginning of this century. There certainly is a basis for this fear although the fear itself can be exaggerated. It requires us to do what we can to remove that fear through wise and carefully considered policies based on long range considerations of true national interest rather than short range considerations of prejudice or perhaps even immediate advantage, or what may seem to be immediate advantage. I suggest that the dangers to which our cultural and non-material life are being exposed today are as great if not greater than those facing control of our economic development. Indeed, the two fears and the two results are closely connected.
This situation has been very well and reasonably described in the report of the royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences which the Liberal government appointed in 1949. I should like to quote from page 18, paragraph 26, of that report on this particular point. It reads:
American influences on Canadian life to say the least are impressive. There should be no thought of interfering with the liberty of all Canadians to enjoy them. Cultural exchanges are excellent in themselves. They widen the choice of the consumer and provide stimulating competition for the producer. It cannot be denied, however, that a vast and disproportionate amount of material coming from a single alien source may stifle rather than stimulate our own creative effort; and, passively accepted without any standard of comparison, this may weaken critical faculties. We are now spending millions to maintain a national independence which would be nothing but an empty shell without a vigorous and distinctive cultural life. We have seen that we have its elements in our traditions and in our history; we have made important progress, often aided by American generosity. We must not be blind, however, to the very present danger of permanent dependence.
That consideration should, I think, be a major preoccupation on the part of the government and all of us in respect of any change that may be recommended in Canadian radio and television policy. We have been led to believe from reports outside this house that some such change is shortly to be recommended. Indeed, it is perhaps true that it is in the field of broadcasting that the possibilities mentioned in the report which I
Radio and Television
have just read of United States influence becoming too powerful and too dominant are greatest. The existence-indeed, the very fortunate existence-of two main language groups; our great area combined with our small and scattered population makes the effective discharge by government of its national responsibilities in this field both difficult and expensive as my hon. friend, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) pointed out two or three weeks ago in what I referred to as a very interesting and, I thought, sensible statement.
The easy way out of this responsibility -just as the easy way out of our transportation responsibilities in this country 80 or so years ago-would have been to have relied on the United States or on policies that would have brought us under United States control in this important field. I wish to read what the Massey report said on this point at page 23, paragraph 3:
The easy and obvious answer soon appeared.
That refers to the answer to our problem of radio and television. Radio was the main concern in early days and the television problem was just emerging at the time of this commission. I continue:
In the United States the new industry of radio was growing phenomenally. Men of enterprise quickly mastered the early techniques and enlisted and adapted an astonishing amount and variety of talent for the new medium. Commercial returns justified their investment. Here, it seemed, was the solution to Canada's problem. With easy access to the south, American programs could be channelled in to Canada inexpensively through stations along the border. Canadians could again feast heartily and cheaply on American bounty, this time without even an obligation to return thanks. It was then that some Canadians began to think that history was about to repeat itself in a new and alarming form.
I suggest that we in this house and indeed in Canada can be grateful to those leaders in both parties who refused to take this easy way out at that time and who, as Canadians had done before them in other spheres of national development, chose the harder but the better course in this great work of nation building by following perhaps a more difficult, but a Canadian way.
I should like to briefly trace for a few minutes the development of Canadian broadcasting policy in the search for this the Canadian way, the Canadian answer to the problems that are inherent in this matter. National policy in this field of broadcasting began, as hon. members know, with the appointment of the Aird commission in 1928 and the principle which that commission adopted as its guide, on which subsequent policy was based and which, I suggest, must still be followed, was expressed by the commission

Radio and Television
in these words which may be found in the report of that body:
In a country of the vast geographical dimensions of Canada, broadcasting will undoubtedly become a great force in fostering a national spirit and interpreting national citizenship.
In due time the report of the Aird commission appeared and it was implemented in part in 1932, but in the main in 1936, through the Canadian Broadcasting Act, which is the legislative basis for a national broadcasting policy in this country. However, one important recommendation of the Aird commission was not implemented. Private broadcasting stations were not absorbed by the government corporation, as the Aird commission had recommended, but rather were integrated into the national system, experience having shown that the private stations could perform important services as part of that national system but not if separate from or aloof from it.
Then the next stage in the development of Canadian policy in this field, at least the next stage which I venture to mention, is the report of the Massey commission, 1951, from which I have already quoted. That commission, as hon. members probably know, reviewed what was being done in this field in the United Kingdom, France, United States and in our own country. It examined complaints received from private broadcasters and it analysed very carefully-and I think myself very fairly-the public interest aspect of broadcasting policy. It restated and it reconfirmed the basic principles and practices of radio policy that had already been laid down in Canada. As we contemplate at this time possible changes in broadcasting policy I think, Mr. Speaker, it is worth recalling what the Massey report had to say in this regard because these are principles on which I think we should base our policy at this time. They are principles which are certainly accepted as the basis for policy by the official opposition. On page 283 of the report we find this, and I read these passages in hearty and complete agreement:
Broadcasting in Canada, in our view, is a public service directed and controlled in the public interest by a body responsible to parliament. Private citizens are permitted to engage their capital and their energies in this service, subject to the regulations of this body. That these citizens should be assured of just and equal treatment, that they should enjoy adequate security or compensation for the actual monetary investments they are permitted to make, is apparent. But that they enjoy any vested right to engage in broadcasting as an industry, or that they have any status except as part of the national broadcasting system, is to us inadmissible.
Then, on page 284 of the report we find this:
The only status of private broadcasters is as part of the national broadcasting system.

Then, paragraph 32 reads:
We wish to recognize fully the private stations as important elements within the framework of our national system. But we are resolutely opposed to any compromise of the principle on which the system rests and should rest. Radio has been the greatest single factor in creating and in fostering a sense of national unity. It has enormous powers to debase and to elevate public understanding and public taste. Believing as we do that it is an essential instrument for the promotion of unity and of general education in the nation, we cannot accept any suggestions which would impair the principles on which our present national system is based.
Mr. Speaker, the Massey commission in short recognized and confirmed that the responsibility of government in this field should be along the lines followed in the United Kingdom and in France but rejected in the United States. We think those principles, as laid down in that report, were sound and wise.
Then we come to the report of the Fowler commission on broadcasting set up, I think, in 1955. That was the next and the last investigation of radio and television in this country, perhaps not the last but the latest, and it was concerned primarily with the television aspects of broadcasting which had made very great strides in Canada since the Massey report. The Fowler report was presented to this house in March, 1957, shortly before parliament dissolved for a general election. That report, the latest report we have on the subject, expressed in strong and clear terms the same fear of undue and damaging United States influences in the television field, as the Massey commission, in its report had previously expressed. It pointed out that the Canadian situation visa-vis the United States in this field makes our position and our problem a unique one in the world, as indeed the Minister of National Revenue has already indicated to the house. It underlined that there was a very real danger in the development of television in this country of Canadian stations becoming what I might call branch plants of United States networks. Perhaps the house will permit me to read from the Fowler report one or two excerpts that deal with this point. On page 7 the Fowler report has this to say:
One of the special factors affecting Canadian broadcasting-
And I have already mentioned this. I continue:
-is the sheer size of the country in relation to its population. We have today in Canada more than 2 million television receivers, each of which is within range of one of the 38 Canadian television stations. In New York-
That is New York city, I take it.
-there are seven television stations whose signals can reach nearly 41 million receiving sets.

Page 8 of the report has this to say:
No other country is similarly helped and embarrassed by the close proximity of the United States. Much that is good and valuable can come from this closeness; there is an increasingly rich fare of programs on both radio and television available at relatively low cost from the United States. Much of this we cannot hope to duplicate and we would be poorer if we did not have it available as part of our total program supply.
But as a nation we cannot accept, in these powerful and persuasive media, the natural and complete flow of another nation's culture without danger to our national identity.
Then, on pages 10 and 11 there are these extracts:
We cannot choose between a Canadian broadcasting system controlled by the state and a Canadian competitive system in private hands. The choice is between a Canadian state-controlled program with some flow of programs east and west across Canada, with some Canadian content and the development of a Canadian sense of identity, at a substantial public cost, and a privately-owned system which the forces of economics will necessarily make predominantly dependent on imported American radio and television programs.
On page 11 we find the following:
If we are unwilling or unable to provide quite substantial amounts from public funds-
And we know they are substantial.
-for such a broadcasting system there is little point in having any public agency engaged in the broadcasting and distribution of radio and television programs, and individual private stations will necessarily become outlets for American networks and programs. This would result not because the private broadcasters are unpatriotic citizens or because they lack a sense of Canadian consciousness or responsibility; it would result from economic pressures on the private operator which make it easy and inexpensive to import American programs and difficult and costly to produce any substantial volume of Canadian programs.
Mr. Speaker, there is the dilemma, and the principles which should underly government policy in resolving that dilemma have been laid down now by more than one commission, as I have stated, and have been followed by governments.
We on this side at this time, wholeheartedly subscribe to these principles and we suggest that there must be no weakening in regard to them. Moreover, the Fowler commission does make certain recommendations which in the opinion of the commission do not violate or weaken the essential principles that have been stated but which will in its opinion improve broadcasting, remove certain grievances and strengthen certain weaknesses in the present system.
For a few moments, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention some of these recommendations of the Fowler commission, some of the views they expressed in their report concerning them and give you my own reaction to those recommendations and views. The first,
Radio and Television
of course, is that public control and regulation of broadcasting is an essential and proper function of parliament exercised not directly but through a state agency or regulatory body. We agree with that. We feel, as commissions that have investigated this matter in the past have felt, that broadcasting is not and in the nature of things cannot be safely considered to be an ordinary business undertaking similar to the publication of a newspaper, a magazine, a popular song or a play. Therefore it does indeed come within the public domain and must be considered in any governmental approach to it, in any parliamentary approach to it, as such.
The Fowler report points out, and rightly I think, that no one has ever argued, at least before any of the commission and I do not think before any of the parliamentary committees, against technical control, against regulations for the allocation of channels and frequencies, against measures to prevent the unauthorized use of airwaves and all that kind of thing. The argument, and it certainly has been an argument and perhaps continues to be, is over the extent to which there should be regulation and control and how that regulation and control should be exercised.
Freedom, of course, in this as in other fields of human activity is very important but the Fowler commission on page 36 of its report states that the most important freedom in this particular medium is "the freedom of the public to enjoy a broadcasting system which provides the largest possible outlet for the widest possible range of information, entertainment and ideas." We agree with that.

speechtext:
That is page 36 of the report where it deals with the question of freedom in its application to broadcasting and television.
The report also states that there must be a single radio and television broadcasting system of which all stations in the country are a part and which will be controlled, regulated and supervised, not directly by government but through a delegated authority responsible to parliament and that in this national system three elements must be considered. The first is the private stations. The second is the publicly operated and controlled Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the third element is a board, however constituted, responsible to parliament and directing and supervising the whole national system.
I should like for a moment to look at these three elements in turn with special reference again to the recommendations and views of the Fowler commission in respect of them. The first element is the private stations. The

Radio and Television
Fowler report emphasizes, and I agree with the emphasis, the importance of the private stations in the national system. Indeed, as members who have read the report will know, and I am sure most members have, the commission was especially preoccupied with the position of the private stations with regard to television.
The report points out in this connection, and quite rightly, that a television licence today in a large Canadian city is, to use the expression of the report itself, a rich plum, and a grant of such a licence imposes a difficult responsibility on government. Furthermore, as I suppose I have already indicated in some of the excerpts I have read from the reports of previous commissions, once that licence is granted there will be a heavy economic pressure on such a private television station to become an outlet for a United States network, especially as such a station would not, I suppose, be likely to join a C.B.C. station in the same city as an outlet of the Canadian national system.
Nevertheless, the Fowler commission does recommend and makes a strong case for abandoning the single channel, as it has been called, or monopoly policy which has been followed in the past by granting in appropriate circumstances, and I emphasize those words, a licence for a private television station in cities where the C.B.C. now operates a television station. The Fowler report agrees that it was deisrable to have one station for as many areas as possible before there should be two stations in any one area but now, the commission thinks, enough progress to this end has been made to justify a change of policy.
But the commission does not stop there. It emphasizes that this change should be brought about gradually and with very great care indeed so as to avoid, for instance, the mistakes that were made in the early days of radio of duplication between private and C.B.C. stations. The necessity for care is underlined not only by the factor I have just mentioned but also by the fact that in Canada today, as hon. members know, there are only 12 very high frequency channels that are assigned to our country. Only 12 are available and that makes them, as I have already indicated, assets of very great value and very great national importance. Therefore the Fowler commission because of these considerations not only advocates care in implementing this change of policy but emphasizes that private competing stations when licensed should be subject to previously determined regulations which would require a minimum standard of Canadian program performance and which would bring them

under some control in respect of such things as advertising. The commission has some very interesting sentences on this particular matter and perhaps before I quote them, Mr. Speaker, I may be permitted to call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
At six o'clock I had been discussing the Fowler report and the recommendations and views in that report concerning the three elements which should constitute the national broadcasting system and the power to regulate and control broadcasting, I had indicated that the Fowler report, while agreeing that there should be modification of the single station policy with regard to television, also emphasized that this change should be brought about very carefully. Its views in that regard are, I think, both interesting and important so far as the private broadcasting element in the system is concerned. I venture to put one or two of these views on the record. For instance, at page 230 of this report, the commission had this to say:
It has been said that available television channels not now in use are rare and precious natural resources that should be preserved for some use in the future. Because the number of unused channels allocated to Canada and practically usable at the present stage of television development is limited, we agree that great care should be exercised in granting licences for these scarce resources. But we think they should not be left idle if they can be used effectively for the benefit of the Canadian people. As with other scarce natural resources, they should not be wasted but neither should they be hoarded.
Then again, in counselling care in granting competing television licences where C.B.C. stations are now operating, at page 235 of its report the commission had this to say:
If the level of performance practically possible under today's conditions is substantially lower than the level determined by the board of broadcast governors to be desirable, Canada would do better to wait for alternative television service.
In short, Mr. Speaker, while the commission recommended-and I have no quarrel with the recommendation-that the policy with regard to the single station for television in any one Canadian city should be modified, it also emphasized that the implementation of this modification should be made with great care.
I now want to say a few words about the second, the public element in the national broadcasting system, which is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and which has, as

we all know, special responsibilities for operating its own stations in the national interest and at present for controlling the whole broadcasting system in this country. This latter function is, of course, a more controversial one. In its report the Fowler commission confirms the good record of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation without suggesting that it is perfect or has been perfect or has not made mistakes or indeed that it cannot be improved. At page 127 of its report the commission has this to say:
Despite a good deal of propaganda directed against the C.B.C. and the Canadian broadcasting system, the results of all past inquiries have been remarkably consistent in giving general approval to Canada's performance and achievements in this field, and it will be seen that the present commission is no exception to this trend.
We on this side of the house also feel that the record of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation over the years has been good, that it has made a distinguished contribution to national development and has operated in the national interest. If that is the case-and I think it is the case-then I think we owe a great debt of gratitude to the chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Mr. Davidson Dunton, who has recently resigned, for the work he has done over the years and for the tact, wisdom, patience and intelligence he has shown in a job which, it seems to me, in complexity and difficulty is second to none in our country. I should like to pay my tribute to the work he has done in this capacity since he was chosen for this position a good many years ago. I am sure he will be missed by the corporation.
It seems to me that the corporation, by its record, stands up well in comparison with broadcasting companies or corporations, public or private, in any other country. It certainly has had to face some terrific problems. Some of these are inherent in the nature of broadcasting. Some of them are peculiar to broadcasting in this country where there are, as I tried to point out this afternoon, some special difficulties. Some of them arise out of the almost furious pace of growth and development in Canada to meet the desires or indeed-and I do not think it is an exaggeration to say this-the demands of the Canadian people.
I suppose it is true to say that growth in the field of television has been faster in Canada than in any other country in the world until today we have reached a position where, so the Fowler report tells us, 97 per cent of the Canadian population are covered by radio and in the space of a very few years 80 per cent of the people are covered by television. Indeed, in four years, I think it is, the number of television sets in this
Radio and Television
country has increased from a few hundred to 2.3 million. No wonder there were, and still are, headaches and growing pains in broadcasting in Canada. I suppose these are increased or are to be increased by the desirability of raising the figure of radio coverage to approximately 100 per cent and television to the objective laid down in the Fowler commission report of at least 90 per cent.
Attaining that latter figure of 90 per cent of our people to be covered by television will be a difficult and expensive proposition under present conditions; and, as the report points out, it will require the establishment of a number of Canadian low-power repeater stations in areas which are not now reached by television but which should be reached by television. The Fowler commission also makes the point, and it is one surely which we can all support.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation . . . should have its task clearly defined,-
I quote from the report at page 160:
-should know the limits beyond which it is not expected to go, and should have the means and the power to discharge that task within those limits.
That brings us to the very core of the problem, as I see it, namely the responsibilities and the resources of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. At present it certainly has definite and very large responsibilities for the provision of national programs and for ensuring that the whole system, public and private, shall be truly national and be guided in its operation in all sectors by national considerations.
For that purpose the corporation has been given certain general powers of regulation and control of the whole system, with which I will try to deal when I come to the third element of the system. For that purpose, even if changes are made in the present system with respect to responsibility for control the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation requires and will continue to require not only large funds with which to meet its obligations but surely it should also have some assurance of the receipt of what it will require over several years, certainly over a longer period than one year. The reconciliation of this requirement and this assurance with considerations of strict economy and parliamentary control is a very difficult problem indeed and one which, I assume, is before the government at the present moment.
I am always very happy indeed to help in the search for any solution of any problem and perhaps what I have to say about this may be of some assistance to the minister in this regard.

Radio and Television
There is no doubt in anyone's mind about the mounting cost to the treasury of the discharge of the responsibilities I have mentioned; there is no doubt about our desire as members of parliament to keep these costs down to the minimum required for the effective discharge of the policies we have laid down. In last year's estimates we voted approximately $27 million for broadcasting and another $16 million for statutory expenditures -approximately $42 million in all

and in this year's estimates the government is providing for $491 million and $12 million statutory expenditures which are provided by the excise tax of 15 per cent on television sets and parts. That is a very large sum of money; something over $61 million in our estimates for broadcasting in Canada.
Some time ago the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation estimated-and this perhaps puts the figures in proper perspective in terms of the services performed-that the cost of television was about $15 per television home per year and that it had been running pretty close to that, though I suspect it will soon be above that figure. However, I venture to say that perhaps no expenditure of $15 per home could bring so much in the way of information, enlightenment and entertainment. I personally felt last night, when watching television for one hour, from ten o'clock to eleven o'clock, that I got back a good proportion of that $15 in that one hour. Therefore we should not begrudge the corporation the necessary amount of money to enable it to do its job, provided that that job is well effectively and economically done. That of course is the question.
It seems pretty clear that if broadcasting services-radio or television-increase, the cost is of course going to increase also. Indeed I have suggested one respect in which these services may perhaps have to increase in extending the television coverage to a greater part of this country. It is also clear that if these extensions are made the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation cannot do its job without some assured and firm basis for its operational and its capital financing.
The Fowler report gives its own estimate of the amount of money which will be required over the period of years up to 1962 and those figures are very, very large. I believe they include the extension of television hours, which may not be as essential as some other changes; the introduction of colour television, which may not be too essential at this time, and the extension of television coverage to 90 per cent, which perhaps is more important than the other two changes.
I come now to the third and last element of this national broadcasting system, that of control and regulation which is now vested

in the chairman and board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Strong exception has in fact been taken in this house to one operating agency, namely the C.B.C., having too much power over other operating and competing agencies, namely the private stations. In other words, that the corporation in these matters of regulation and control is taking the position-and it has been put this way in this house-of both judge and jury.
In my view, from the study I have been able to give to this question, the present system has not worked too badly in practice. I do not think the C.B.C. has abused its powers but I am inclined to agree that the principle, as a principle, is open to some objection. The Fowler commission presumably came to the same conclusion because they recommend a change in this regard without however-and I think this is important-compromising the essential principle that one national system should be ensured. To reconcile that principle with the change which it thinks desirable the commission recommended in its report a separate board, of what it called broadcasting governors, to consist of fifteen members appointed for five-year terms, at least one of whom would be from each of the five major regions of Canada. It is not, in this recommendation, to be a board like the board of transport commissioners, which is a fulltime official board. It is to be a part-time board and even the chairman is to be a part-time appointee. Naturally he and the other members of the executive committee would have to spend more time in Ottawa than would the remainder of the board.
The report emphasizes that the membership is to be highly qualified and is to be independent of the government in the same way as, say, the board of directors of the Bank of Canada are independent of the government. I certainly agree with the commission in this respect. Independence is stressed as being essential in the recommendation made both with regard to public and private elements of the system would be responsible to this board of broadcasting governors which would in its constitution, its functions and in its authority be quite apart from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; it would, as I understand it, itself have no operating: responsibility but it would have control over the national system and over broadcasting policy. It would be responsible for making and enforcing regulations. In exercising this control, in its supervisory functions and, in enforcing minimum standards of performance, the board-the report says-should not be rigid or unduly interfering or attempt to interpret the public interest in too limiting and narrow a manner. I think that is a very

wise safeguard, as are those safeguards recommended against an unfair exercise of regulatory functions. In my own view, and I think in the view of a good many people who have studied this matter, it would be a mistake if we changed our broadcasting policy so that we had two boards, one the kind of board I have been mentioning and another board for the C.B.C. itself; in other words, one as at present, which would be concerned with programs and performance of the C.B.C. alone and a second board which would be a small full-time board concerned mainly with licensing new radio and television stations, increases of power for stations and such things, but without the authority to control standards of current performance or excessive commercialism in the whole system.
I am suggesting we should be making a mistake if we left the C.B.C. under its own board and then attempted to set up a full time board concerning mainly with licensing problems and only in a secondary way with the control and regulation of the whole system. It seems to me two such boards of that kind would be wasteful and overlapping. On the other hand, one small full-time board-I will compare it with the board of transport commissioners though the analogy is by no means perfect-with all the power to regulate and control might, in my opinion, prejudice the national system, based as it is on the special responsibilities of the C.B.C. and the prior position of the C.B.C., because of those responsibilities, in that system, which in my view should be maintained.
On the other hand, the role of a part-time independent board of broadcast governors would not be primarily administrative or technical but, within existing legislation, would keep broadcast policy in line generally with public opinion and protect the public interest in this vital matter. That is the kind of board we on this side of the house would prefer.
In conclusion, may I say that we approve in general the recommendations of the Fowler commission and we feel they might well form the basis of any new legislation on the subject, and I say that without accepting them in all their detail. The attitude of the official opposition on this most important problem can be summed up by the following broad principles of policy. In the first place, we feel that private radio and television stations have an important role to play in the field of broadcasting in Canada, not as an independent network but as a part of a single and integrated national system operating under the control and supervision of a public regulatory body to make sure-and I am quoting now from
Radio and Television
the Fowler report-that programs are responsive to Canadian needs and adapted to Canadian conditions and that the public rather than any private interest should prevail.
In the second place, the C.B.C. must continue to play a dominant role in our national system of broadcasting. In order to be in a position to perform that function effectively it must be completely free of government interference and be ultimately responsible only to parliament; it must also receive adequate funds, not merely on a year-to-year basis but, subject always to parliament control, in such a way as to be able to plan in advance the development of its services.
The proper operation and development of such a national system of broadcasting will be costly and will involve increased public expenditures in the future. It is imperative that we should be prepared to meet this responsibility if we want to grow and develop as a distinct nation. I should like in this respect to quote the very sound and serious warning given to us all in this house by Michael Barkway in a C.B.C. capital report on June 29, 1958:
Nationwide television will probably involve costs proportionate to the unique contribution it can make towards developing and informing a Canadian point of view. If ever we decide it is not worth the price-that we could get along just as well with free American programs-then it will be high time to put your money elsewhere and prepare to abandon ship. There are quicker ways to destroy Canada, but none more decisive: because this would mean declaring that we don't really care any more.
It is important that the position of the government on these matters and particular in regard to the recommendations of the Fowler commission should be stated clearly, and stated soon. Delay and doubt about this matter is creating difficulties and uncertainties in this field. The Fowler report has been in the hands of government for well over a year. Where does the government stand on it? Is, for instance, the board of governors of the C.B.C. being abolished by default? The announcement in the speech from the throne has only added to this uncertainty, especially in the light of past statement, because it says merely this:
There will be placed before you a proposal to establish a new agency to regulate broadcasting in Canada and to ensure that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the privately owned broadcasting stations work effectively together to constitute a national system to provide satisfactory television and radio services to all Canadians within reach. Related amendments to the Radio Act will also be proposed.
We think that this parliament, many weeks after that speech from the throne was

Radio and Television
delivered, is now entitled to a clear statement of government policy with regard to the implications of that paragraph. By moving this amendment we hope to get that statement from the government, and therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) the following:
That all the words after the word "That" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor: "this house regrets the government has not yet presented its proposals for the regulation and financing of radio and television broadcasting and thereby removing the uncertainty as to the future of public and private broadcasting in Canada.

I am sure that in that part of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition we in the C.C.F. can heartily concur. Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman could see my notes he would think a chicken with wet, muddy feet had tracked across the page. Before proceeding further I think I should join with the Leader of the Opposition in expressing our admiration for the valuable services rendered to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation over a period of 12 or 13 years if I remember correctly and also to the Canadian people by Mr. Dunton. It was not an easy task to be at the head of that organization and I am convinced that it was not made any less easy at times by the vigorous criticisms of some of the hon. gentlemen who now sit on the government side of the house. We wish Mr. Dunton every success in his new undertaking as president of Carleton University.
Throughout the years the question of the C.B.C. is one that has drawn a great deal of attention in this house and provoked much interest and comment in the country. That has been indicated by the fact, if I remember correctly, that there have been 13 parliamentary committees over the years studying the administration of the C.B.C and some

three royal commissions. The Aird commission was the first in 1928. The Massey commission also made a study of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the latest, the Fowler commission, reported on the subject in 1957. I am not going to repeat what the Leader of the Opposition had to say with respect to the Aird commission. We in this group agree with most of his comments in connection with that commission. However, I do wish to refer briefly to some of what we consider were the inadequacies of the Massey commission with respect to its report in so far as it referred to radio broadcasting and we must all realize that the situation has changed a great deal since the time of that report.
While it was an excellent report and covered the field quite comprehensively under the circumstances that prevailed at the time there were three major omissions in the Massey commission report from the point of view of this group. The first was that it failed to suggest that higher standards should be required by private stations. We in this group think that is a question that should be given very serious consideration by this parliament and those that are charged with the responsibility of administering radio in Canada. We also do not believe that newspapers should be given radio or television licences and the Massey report failed to mention that.
The third suggestion omitted from the report which in our view would have been worth while and necessary was that the board of governors be more qualified. I am not making any undue criticisms of the board of governors and their services in the past. The experience of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in radio and television throughout the years has been evolutionary. We feel that the board of governors should be more qualified to analyse and understand programs, administrative procedures and to understand to a greater degree than was possible in the past the very complex technical difficulties that are related to making decisions in respect to radio broadcasting and television.

ability, divorced from the direct administration of the organization, have some degree of technical competence to pass on some of these very complicated and difficult problems particularly when it comes to the question of applications for two stations in one city or the necessary things that are required to give radio coverage in certain areas and questions of that nature.
With respect to the report of the Fowler commission I-or rather, we in this group- think it is most comprehensive. I am not very much given to saying "I" but one slips into the habit and when speaking on a subject like this I want it understood that I am speaking for the members of this group. We are not given to putting ourselves forward as individuals. We submerge our personalities to the common good, you know.

This report indicates that the commission made a very thorough and exhaustive study of the subject. The report also indicates the very widespread support for the C.B.C. that exists in this country. In that connection I wish to refer to a bulletin that was sent to my office by the Canadian broadcasting league which has lately been revived, as I understand it. The bulletin contains a paragraph which refers to national support for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and which reads as follows:
The report of the royal commission on broadcasting 1957, signed by R. M. Fowler, president, Canadian Pulp and Paper Association; Edmond Turcotte, ambassador; and James Stewart, president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, states (page 11):
"The overwhelming weight of evidence submitted to us-compelled us to report that Canadians wish to have a Canadian broadcasting system . . . want to keep some part of their broadcasting fare Canadian, and are willing within reason, to pay for it."
My comment in this connection would be that there is clear evidence of the value of the work that has been done throughout the years by those who have been charged with the administration of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The second point in this bulletin reads:
Some 245 organizations representing over six million Canadians submitted briefs of many points of view; but:
"there was virtual unanimity in favour of a Canadian broadcasting system, supported by moneys from the federal treasury."
Then, this report goes on to list a number of organizations that made representations to the commission and I find eight national religious organizations, and then some 10

Radio and Television
French-Canadian organizations, universities and various well known French-Canadian societies, and some 10 labour organizations, headed by the Canadian labour congress; some 9 women's organizations, such as the national council of women of Canada, the Canadian federation of university women, the I.O.D.E., women's institutes, and so on. I am very pleased to see that because I think it is a good omen that the women of Canada should commence to take a great interest in a subject such as this.
Then, I come to agricultural organizations; I see 12 are noted, several of them of national scope, the Canadian federation of agriculture, the co-operative union of Canada and so on. Then, we come to organizations representative of music, drama and the arts, and here we find nine organizations, including the Canadian arts council, the national ballet guild, the Canadian council of authors and artists, the dominion drama festival, the Canadian league of composers, and so on.
Then, interestingly enough, we have eight private radio broadcasting stations, apparently making representations in support of the C.B.C. as the publicly owned body representing the people of Canada to carry on radio, and then some 16 educational organizations such as the Canadian home and school and parent-teachers federation, Canadian association for adult education, national advisory council on school broadcasting and so on, and several of the universities across Canada including this list.
I think, this indicates very clearly that while as the Leader of the Opposition said, there is no organization or group that does not make mistakes under very difficult conditions where we have had this development of television, a very expensive medium of communication in recent years, changed technical conditions, procedures and things of that sort, the C.B.C. has done a wonderful job in this country, which is recognized by the Canadian people as a whole.
I am going to speak very briefly, Mr. Speaker, because as I said before I do not want to repeat what was said by the Leader of the Opposition. This report does make some very concrete recommendations, the first of which on page 13 is as follows:
That the mixed Canadian system of public and private ownership is here to stay.
One would almost think that that was taken out of the C.C.F. program, Mr. Speaker. Here is a demonstration of the workability, the efficiency and the public accord given to a mixed economy, the first step in that direction on a national scale. Recommendation No. 2 reads:
That the state agency may grow, as Canada grows, but its functions are not to be extended to
[Mr. Herridge.l
do the whole job of providing radio and television services to Canadians.
Quite rightly so. We have found this mixture of public and private enterprise in Canada on the basis of the C.C.F. proposals in this direction throughout the years very suitable indeed. We suggest the necessary direction and control of major policy, but still leaving flexibility for local initiative, local control, and things of that sort.
The third recommendation reads:
That private stations should individually be required to justify the continued grant of a valuable public franchise and that some may lose their licences because of a shabby performance, but private operators should stop worrying about the bogey of nationalization that has filled them with suspicion and fear in the past.
We in this group do not see much to object to in this paragraph. The fourth recommendation reads:
That, for the foreseeable future, we will continue to have a single broadcasting system in which all Canadian radio and television stations, public and private, present and future, will be integral parts, regulated and controlled by an agency representing the public interest and responsible to parliament.
One would almost think that this paragraph was written at the C.C.F. national convention. You know, Mr. Speaker, it is strange when somebody else says these things and writes these words. Then, such words as "control" and "regulate" are perfectly respectable, but if we should include such words in a portion of our program or of our manifesto, or things of that sort, the challenge of dictatorship, tyranny and all the rest of it is immediately hurled at us. Therefore, you can see that once again, Mr. Speaker, the members of the other parties in this house and even distinguished people employed by the government in this country on behalf of Canadians are infected by the language, the philosophy and the outlook of the C.C.F.
